newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall as oil prices jump, bonds fall.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall as oil prices jump, bonds fall.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell Wednesday, hurt by a jump in crude oil prices that sparked inflation jitters in the bond market.
The Dow Jones industrial average dropped 68.08 points to 7,689.98, giving back a large chunk of Tuesday's 153-point gain.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,558 to 1,254 on heavy volume of 603 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Stocks spent the day swinging sharply from the plus to the minus column but the market took a sharp downturn on news that OPEC reached an agreement to limit overproduction, which is meant to boost oil prices and could feed inflation.

Wall Street's concern about the impact of higher oil prices was reflected in the inflation-sensitive bond market, where the 30-year Treasury fell 19/32, or $5.94 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.74 percent from 6.69 percent Tuesday. The price and yield move in opposite directions.
Meanwhile, crude oil for August delivery rose 49 cents to $19.52 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
OPEC, which met in Vienna, said the 11-member oil cartel had agreed to retain its 25.03 million barrels per day ceiling until the end of the year.
More significantly, it said that OPEC members agreed to stick to their export quotas, which implied that the producers would stop pumping the 2 million barrels a day in excess of the quota limit.
"We have a very high level of commitment ... one hundred percent," said Saudi Arabian Oil Minister Ali Naimi.
The Libyan president of OPEC, Abdullah Salem al-Badri, said that production "should go down" as a result of promises given in Vienna.

Analysts said the financial markets were also spooked by rumours that a major seller of Treasury bonds might be a foreign central bank. An unidentified seller unloaded $1 billion of 10-year notes, which sent the bond market reeling.

"The market is very nervous. The Dow travelled ... back and forth today with nothing concrete. There were rumours of foreigners selling in bonds and crude rose slightly after OPEC," said said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.

Analysts said comments by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin Wednesday did not calm the markets, which got rocked on Monday after a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto sparked fears Japan might sell some of its large holdings of Treasury bonds. Rubin said there was no reason to expect such sales and that the market could absorb them if they occurred.
"Why would he say that except to possibly cushion a blow? Market players are very sceptical about remarks like that," one analyst said.
Japan is the biggest foreign buyer of Treasury bonds, with holdings of about $300 billion, and if it started selling, long-term interest rates could jump, hurting the U.S. economy.
Traders said the market's swings indicated that investors were nervous.

"The recent volatility is due to the increasing skittishness of market participants. It's normally not a very good thing. But it tends to happen around highs and lows," said Harry Laubscher, an analyst at Tucker Anthony.
The shares of oil companies fell, with Exxon Corp. falling 1-9/16 , Chevron Corp. losing 7/16 to 73-13/16 and Texaco Inc. off 1/2 at 111-3/8.
Almost all of the 30 Dow components closed lower, except Sears Roebuck & Co., up 2/16 at 53-15/16 and Minnesota Mining & Manufacturing Co., up 1/4 at 101-1/4 and AT&T Corp.
AT&T rose 1/16 at 37 amid strength in telecom stocks.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 6.19 points to 1,446.24.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks lost 7.35 to 888.99. The American Stock Exchange index slipped 0.62 to 619.24.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks fell 3.27 to 462.90. The average share was down 31 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 8,407.205, down 53.650 or 0.63 percent.
